q: An adhesive is best described as a substance that:
o: Gives a permanent colour to a fibre
Joins two surfaces together and resists their separation
Protects a metal surface from corrosion
x: Adhesives (glues) hold materials together by sticking to their surfaces. A substance that colours a fibre is a dye, and one that speeds a reaction is a catalyst.

q: Which of the following is a natural adhesive?
x: Starch paste comes from plant starch and is used for paper, bookbinding and wallpaper. Epoxy resins, cyanoacrylates and polyvinyl acetate are synthetic adhesives.

q: Animal glue, used for wood and bookbinding, is obtained by:
o: Boiling animal bones, hides and hooves
x: Boiling bones and hides breaks down their collagen into gelatin-like glue. Polymerising vinyl acetate gives the synthetic white glue PVA, and phenol with methanal gives a phenol–formaldehyde resin.

q: Casein glue is a natural adhesive made from:
x: Casein, the main protein of milk, is separated from skimmed milk and made into a glue that is used for wood and labels. It is a protein-based natural adhesive.

q: Cyanoacrylate adhesive ('super glue') sets within seconds because it:
o: Loses solvent very quickly by evaporation
Polymerises rapidly when it meets traces of moisture on the surfaces
Must be melted and then cooled
x: The cyanoacrylate monomer polymerises very quickly when touched by tiny amounts of water on surfaces, forming a strong bond. It is a one-part adhesive, so no hardener or heating is needed.

q: An epoxy adhesive is sold as two tubes whose contents must be mixed just before use. This is because:
o: The two parts are different colours
The resin and the hardener react together to form a hard cross-linked polymer
One tube contains the solvent that must evaporate
The mixture must be heated to melt it
x: Epoxy adhesives are reactive: the resin and hardener react chemically and cure into a rigid, cross-linked solid. This gives very strong bonds to metal, glass and ceramics.

q: Adhesive tapes and sticky labels stick when pressed by hand, without water, solvent or heat. They use:
x: Pressure-sensitive adhesives stay permanently tacky and bond under light pressure. Hot-melts need heat, reactive adhesives need mixing, and animal glue is applied wet and must dry.

q: A glue gun uses an adhesive stick that is solid at room temperature, is applied molten and sets as it cools. This is a:
x: Hot-melt adhesives are thermoplastic: they are melted, applied, and harden on cooling without any chemical reaction. A contact adhesive is spread on both surfaces and allowed to dry before pressing.

q: White wood glue is an emulsion of polyvinyl acetate (PVA) in water. It hardens mainly by:
o: Losing water by evaporation and absorption
Reacting with nitrogen in the air
x: PVA glue is a drying adhesive: as the water evaporates or soaks into the wood or paper, the polymer particles join into a solid film.

q: Which adhesive, once set, cannot be softened again by heating?
x: Epoxy resin cures into a cross-linked thermosetting polymer, which chars rather than softens on heating. Hot-melts, PVA and rubber-based adhesives are thermoplastic and soften when warmed.

q: The group of atoms in a dye molecule that is responsible for its colour is called the:
x: A chromophore, such as –N=N– or –NO₂, absorbs visible light and so gives colour. An auxochrome deepens the colour and helps the dye attach to the fibre.

q: Which group acts as an auxochrome in dye molecules?
x: Auxochromes such as –NH₂ and –OH are not colour-producing by themselves, but they intensify the colour and help the dye bind to fibres. –N=N–, –NO₂ and C=O are chromophores.

q: Azo dyes are so called because their molecules contain the group:
x: Azo dyes contain the –N=N– chromophore linking two aromatic rings. They are the largest group of synthetic dyes; methyl orange is an example.

q: Indigo is a vat dye. Which statement describes how it is applied to cotton?
o: It is applied directly from a hot aqueous solution
It is fixed to the fibre by a metal salt such as alum
It is reduced to a soluble form, applied to the fibre, and then oxidised back by air
It is melted onto the fibre
x: Vat dyes are insoluble in water. They are reduced in an alkaline vat to a soluble leuco form, which soaks into the fibre, and air oxidation then regenerates the insoluble coloured dye inside the fibre.

q: In dyeing, a mordant is:
o: A substance, often a metal salt such as alum, that fixes a dye to the fibre
The coloured part of the dye molecule
A solvent used to dissolve the dye
A reducing agent that makes a vat dye soluble
x: Mordant dyes cannot attach strongly by themselves, so the fibre is treated with a metal salt that forms an insoluble coloured complex with the dye. Alizarin is a classic mordant dye.

q: Acid dyes, which contain –SO₃H or –COOH groups, are mainly used to dye:
x: Wool, silk and nylon contain basic –NH₂ groups that attract the anionic acid dye, so the dye binds well. Polyester is dyed with disperse dyes, and polythene and glass take up dyes poorly.

q: Which of the following is a natural dye obtained from a plant?
x: Indigo was traditionally extracted from the indigo plant. Methyl orange, Congo red and malachite green are synthetic dyes.

q: Congo red can be applied to cotton from a hot aqueous solution without any mordant. It is therefore classed as a:
x: Direct dyes are water-soluble and attach to cellulose fibres such as cotton straight from solution. Vat dyes need reduction and oxidation, and mordant dyes need a metal salt.

q: Methyl orange, used as an indicator in acid–base titrations, belongs by structure to the class of:
x: Methyl orange contains the –N=N– group linking two benzene rings, so it is an azo dye. Its colour changes with pH, which is why it is used as an indicator.

q: Reactive dyes on cotton are very resistant to washing because they:
o: Are held only by weak van der Waals forces
Form covalent bonds with the –OH groups of cellulose
Are insoluble in water at all temperatures
Are fixed by a metal mordant
x: A reactive dye contains a group that reacts with the hydroxyl groups of cellulose, joining the dye to the fibre by a covalent bond. A covalent link cannot be washed out, unlike weaker attractions.

q: Polythene (polyethene) is made by polymerising:
x: Polythene is an addition polymer of ethene, CH₂=CH₂: n CH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ. Ethane has no double bond, so it cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

q: Which statement about addition polymers is correct?
o: A small molecule such as water is lost at each link
The monomers must have two different functional groups
Only aromatic compounds can act as monomers
The polymer has the same empirical formula as its monomer
x: In addition polymerisation, monomers with C=C bonds join without losing any atoms, so the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer. Loss of a small molecule happens in condensation polymerisation.

q: The monomer of PVC is:
x: PVC, polyvinyl chloride, is made from vinyl chloride (chloroethene), CH₂=CHCl. CF₂=CF₂ gives Teflon and CH₂=CHCH₃ gives polypropene.

q: Teflon, used to coat non-stick cooking pans, is made by polymerising:
x: Teflon is polytetrafluoroethene, an addition polymer of CF₂=CF₂. Its strong C–F bonds make it chemically inert and heat-resistant. Chloroethene gives PVC and phenylethene gives polystyrene.

q: Nylon-6,6 is made from:
x: The –NH₂ groups of the diamine react with the –COOH groups of adipic acid, losing water and forming amide links. Ethane-1,2-diol with terephthalic acid gives a polyester, and phenol with methanal gives Bakelite.

q: In the name nylon-6,6, the two numbers show that:
o: Each of the two monomers contains six carbon atoms
The polymer chain has six repeating units
Six molecules of water are lost per repeat unit
x: Hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid each have six carbon atoms, hence 6,6. Only one water molecule is lost for each amide link formed.

q: The polyester fibre Terylene (Dacron) is formed by condensation of ethane-1,2-diol with:
o: Hexanedioic acid, with amide links formed
Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid), with ester links formed
x: The –OH groups of the diol react with the –COOH groups of terephthalic acid, losing water and forming ester (–COO–) links. Amide links are found in nylons.

q: Bakelite, a hard thermosetting plastic used for electrical switches and pan handles, is made from:
x: Phenol and methanal undergo condensation polymerisation, losing water and forming a three-dimensional cross-linked network. The cross-links make Bakelite rigid and stop it softening on heating.

q: Which of the following is a condensation polymer?
x: Nylon-6,6 forms with loss of water as each amide link is made, so it is a condensation polymer. Polythene, PVC and Teflon are addition polymers of alkenes.

q: Which pair consists of two condensation polymers?
x: Polyester forms by loss of water between a diol and a diacid, and Bakelite by loss of water between phenol and methanal. Polythene, PVC and Teflon are all addition polymers, so every other pair contains at least one.

q: A sample of polythene has an average relative molecular mass of 56 000. The average number of ethene units in each chain is (C 12, H 1):
x: Each repeat unit –CH₂–CH₂– has Mr = 28, so the number of units = 56 000/28 = 2000. 4000 comes from wrongly dividing by 14, the mass of one CH₂ group.
